sections.title: The Gateway: How can a few marks on a page put another person's mind inside yours?
sections.html:
Web address: /books/how-books-work/ · Keywords: history of books for beginners, why we read, how writing began, what is literature

Open any book and something strange happens. Black marks on paper turn into a voice in your head. That voice may belong to someone who died two thousand years ago, or who lives on the other side of the world, and for a few hours you think their thoughts.

This short course follows one question in ten small steps: how did humans learn to store minds on a page, and why do we still do it? It goes from storytellers who carried epics in memory, through palm leaves, printing presses and novels, to e-books and AI. Each page takes about two minutes and hands you the next question. You can stop after any page and still leave with a complete answer.

By the end you will be able to:

  • Tell the story of the book in order, from memory to clay to paper to screen.
  • Explain why India wrote on palm leaves and birch bark, and why so many texts were memorised.
  • Say how printing changed religion, science and politics.
  • Explain, with real research, what reading does to the brain.
  • Think clearly about whether e-books and AI will replace books.

sections.title: How did humans tell stories before writing?
sections.html:
Short answer: With memory, rhythm and community. For most of human history, literature was oral: epics, songs, riddles and laws were memorised and performed. Rhyme, metre and repetition were the "storage technology".

Keywords: oral tradition, oral literature, how the Vedas were preserved, bards, storytelling before writing

The oldest library was a human head

Writing is only about 5,000 years old, but people have told stories for as long as they have had language. Before writing, a story survived only if someone remembered it and someone else wanted to hear it. So stories were shaped to be remembered: they used rhythm, rhyme, refrains, stock phrases and vivid images.

India's extraordinary memory

India is the world's great example. The Vedas were composed from roughly 1500 BCE and passed down orally for centuries before they were written. Reciters used patterns such as padapatha (word by word), kramapatha and ghanapatha, which repeat words in different orders like an error-checking code. UNESCO recognised Vedic chanting as an Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2008 (proclaimed 2003).

Bards everywhere

Greek bards sang the Homeric epics. West African griots (jeli) still carry the history of families and kingdoms, including the Epic of Sundiata. In Rajasthan, bhopas sing the epic of Pabuji in front of a painted phad scroll. Tribal communities across India, from the Gonds to the Bhils, keep creation stories and songs in memory.

What oral literature does well

Oral stories change a little with every telling. They belong to the community rather than to one author. They are performed, not just read, so music, gesture and audience all matter.

Remember this: Literature is older than writing; memory and rhythm were the first books.

Next: If stories lived in memory, who first wrote one down, and what was the first "book"?

sections.title: Who wrote the first book?
sections.html:
Short answer: Writing began in Mesopotamia (cuneiform, around 3300–3100 BCE) and Egypt (hieroglyphs) for accounts and records. Among the oldest literary works are the Sumerian hymns of Enheduanna (around 2300 BCE), often called the first named author, and the Epic of Gilgamesh.

Keywords: first book ever written, oldest literature, Epic of Gilgamesh, Enheduanna, history of writing

Writing began with accounts, not poems

The first writing in Sumer recorded grain, sheep and debts on clay tablets. Writing was invented independently in a few places: Mesopotamia, Egypt, China (oracle-bone script, around 1200 BCE) and Mesoamerica. The Indus script (around 2600–1900 BCE) is still undeciphered, so we do not know what it says.

The first named author

Enheduanna, a priestess and daughter of King Sargon of Akkad, wrote hymns to the goddess Inanna around 2300 BCE. She is usually called the first author known by name, and she was a woman.

The first great story

The Epic of Gilgamesh tells of a king who loses his friend Enkidu and searches for immortality. Its stories circulated from around 2100 BCE, and the best-known version was found in the library of King Ashurbanipal at Nineveh (7th century BCE). It even contains a flood story.

What counts as a "book"?

A clay tablet is not a book as we know it. Over time, writing moved to papyrus scrolls (Egypt), bamboo and silk (China), palm leaves and birch bark (India), parchment and finally the codex, the bound book with pages, which spread in the Roman world from the 1st century CE.

Remember this: The first writing was bookkeeping; the first named author was a woman poet, Enheduanna.

sections.title: Why did India write on palm leaves?
sections.html:
Short answer: Because palm leaves were cheap, plentiful and durable in the Indian climate. Scribes wrote on dried talipot or palmyra leaves, and on birch bark (bhojpatra) in the north. Leaves were tied with string through holes; the word grantha (book) comes from "tying".

Keywords: palm leaf manuscripts, bhojpatra, how ancient Indian books were made, grantha meaning, National Mission for Manuscripts

Making a palm-leaf book

Leaves were dried, boiled, smoothed and cut to size. In the south and east, scribes scratched letters with an iron stylus and rubbed in soot or lamp-black so the grooves turned black; this helped shape rounded scripts like Odia and Malayalam, because straight lines would split the leaf. In the north, people often wrote with ink on birch bark or palm leaf.

The Gilgit and Bakhshali manuscripts

The Gilgit manuscripts (birch bark, about the 5th–7th centuries CE) are among the oldest surviving manuscripts in India and include Buddhist texts. The Bakhshali manuscript of mathematics, also on birch bark, contains a dot used as zero; radiocarbon tests in 2017 dated some of its leaves to the 3rd–4th century CE, though scholars still debate its exact age.

A living heritage

Leaves decay, so texts were copied again and again by families, monasteries, temples and Jain bhandars (libraries) such as those at Patan and Jaisalmer. India's National Mission for Manuscripts (2003) estimates that India holds millions of manuscripts, many still uncatalogued.

Paper arrives

Paper, invented in China (traditionally credited to Cai Lun, 105 CE), reached India through Central Asia and was common by the Sultanate and Mughal periods. Mughal workshops produced illustrated manuscripts such as the Hamzanama.

Remember this: India's "books" were tied bundles of leaves, copied again and again, and its scripts were shaped by the stylus.

sections.title: How did printing change the world?
sections.html:
Short answer: Printing made copies cheap and identical. China printed first (woodblock; the Diamond Sutra of 868 CE is the oldest dated printed book). Bi Sheng made movable type around 1040. Johannes Gutenberg's press (around 1450) spread across Europe and helped power the Reformation, the Scientific Revolution and newspapers.

Keywords: history of printing, Gutenberg press, Diamond Sutra, first printing press in India, movable type

Asia first

The Diamond Sutra found at Dunhuang is dated 868 CE. Bi Sheng made clay movable type in Song China, and Korea printed the Jikji with metal movable type in 1377, before Gutenberg.

Gutenberg's revolution

Around 1450 in Mainz, Gutenberg combined metal type, oil-based ink and a screw press. His Bible appeared about 1455. Within fifty years, presses were running in more than 200 European cities, and millions of books had been printed. Martin Luther's pamphlets of 1517 spread fast because of print.

Printing reaches India

Portuguese Jesuits set up a press in Goa in 1556. The first book printed in an Indian script was Tamil: Thambiran Vanakkam (1578). In 1800 the Serampore Mission Press (William Carey) and Fort William College began printing in Bengali, Hindi and many other languages. Newspapers followed: Hicky's Bengal Gazette (1780).

What changed

Ideas could now travel faster than rulers could stop them. Spelling and languages became more standard. Readers could compare identical copies, which helped science. It also made censorship a bigger business.

Remember this: Printing turned books from rare treasures into everyday tools, first in Asia, then explosively in Europe.

Next: Once books were cheap, a new form appeared that worried parents and priests. Why was the novel once called dangerous?

sections.title: Why was the novel once called dangerous?
sections.html:
Short answer: Because it let ordinary readers, especially young women, live other lives in private. In 18th- and 19th-century Europe and India, critics warned that novels corrupted morals and wasted time. The same fear later attached to comics, television, video games and phones.

Keywords: history of the novel, first novel ever, Tale of Genji, Don Quixote, first Indian novel

Where the novel began

There is no single first novel. Murasaki Shikibu's The Tale of Genji (Japan, around 1010) is often called the world's first novel. Cervantes's Don Quixote (1605 and 1615) is called the first modern European novel. Sanskrit had long prose romances: Banabhatta's Kadambari (7th century), whose name became the word for "novel" in Kannada and Marathi.

The fear of novels

In 18th-century England, sermons and newspapers warned that novels made girls dreamy and disobedient. In 19th-century Bengal and Maharashtra, reformers argued about whether novels taught good conduct or bad.

India's first novels

Bengali's Durgeshnandini (Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay, 1865) is often called the first major Indian novel. Earlier candidates include Alaler Gharer Dulal (Peary Chand Mitra, 1857) in Bengali, Pariksha Guru (Lala Srinivas Das, 1882) in Hindi, Indulekha (O. Chandu Menon, 1889) in Malayalam and Rajmohan's Wife (Bankim, 1864) in English.

Why the fear was wrong, and right

Novels did change people. They taught readers to imagine the inner life of someone else, which researchers today link to empathy (BOK-21). That is exactly why rulers and moralists feared them.

Remember this: The novel is a machine for living other lives, and every new storytelling machine is feared at first.

Next: Is poetry older than all of this?

sections.title: Is poetry older than prose?
sections.html:
Short answer: In literature, yes, almost everywhere. The oldest literary works (the Vedas, Gilgamesh, Homer, the Chinese Shijing, Tamil Sangam poems) are in verse, because rhythm helps memory. Prose literature grows later, once writing is common.

Keywords: oldest poetry, why poetry came first, chhanda, metre in poetry, Shijing

Why verse came first

Verse is easier to remember. A line with a fixed beat tells you when you have forgotten a syllable. India built a full science of metre, chhandas, one of the six Vedangas; Pingala's Chandahshastra (before 200 BCE) even uses binary-like patterns of short and long syllables.

Verse for everything

Ancient India wrote medicine, astronomy and grammar in verse. Aryabhata's astronomy (499 CE) is in verse. The Chinese Shijing (Classic of Poetry) collects songs from around 1000 to 600 BCE. Tamil Sangam poetry (roughly 300 BCE to 300 CE) sorts poems into akam (inner life, love) and puram (outer life, war and kings).

Then prose grows up

Prose appears in law codes, commentaries, letters, histories and stories. Sanskrit prose romances, Greek history (Herodotus), Chinese history (Sima Qian) and Arabic prose all grow once writing is common.

Today

Prose dominates bookshops, but poetry survives everywhere people want words to be remembered: songs, slogans, prayers, film lyrics, rap and Instagram poems.

Remember this: Poetry came first because rhythm was memory; prose came when paper did the remembering.

sections.title: Why do some books outlive empires?
sections.html:
Short answer: Because they are copied, taught, translated and loved by many communities for different reasons. A "classic" survives when each generation finds something new in it. Luck, religion, schools and translation all help.

Keywords: what makes a classic, oldest books still read, why classics survive, Panchatantra translations

The Panchatantra's journey

The Panchatantra (animal fables, compiled perhaps around 300 CE) was translated into Middle Persian in the 6th century, then into Arabic as Kalila wa Dimna (Ibn al-Muqaffa, 8th century), then into Hebrew, Latin and most European languages. It is one of the most translated books in history.

The four reasons books survive

  1. Copying communities: monasteries, temples, madrasas, families and later schools kept copying.
  2. Rereadability: the Mahabharata, Homer and Shakespeare say different things to different ages.
  3. Translation: a book in many languages is hard to destroy.
  4. Luck: fire, war and decay destroyed much. The Library of Alexandria's losses and the burning of Nalanda (around 1193) are remembered as warnings.

What we lost

Most ancient literature is lost. We know of hundreds of Greek plays by title only. Many Sanskrit, Tamil and Prakrit works survive only as quotations in other books.

Remember this: A classic is a book that every generation chooses to copy again.

sections.title: What happens in your brain when you read?
sections.html:
Short answer: Reading borrows brain circuits built for vision and speech. A small region on the left side, nicknamed the "letterbox area" by the neuroscientist Stanislas Dehaene, learns to recognise written words. Stories also activate areas used for understanding other people's minds.

Keywords: reading and the brain, Stanislas Dehaene, Maryanne Wolf, deep reading, how children learn to read

The brain was not built to read

Writing is too recent for evolution to have made a reading organ. Instead, as Dehaene explains in Reading in the Brain (2009), a child's brain recycles part of the visual system (the visual word form area) to recognise letters and link them to sounds.

Deep reading

The scholar Maryanne Wolf (Proust and the Squid, 2007; Reader, Come Home, 2018) describes "deep reading": slow, attentive reading that builds inference, analogy and empathy. She worries that skimming on screens trains a shallower habit, though research on this is still developing.

Stories and other minds

Psychologists Keith Oatley and Raymond Mar have found links between reading fiction and the ability to understand others' feelings, though how strong the effect is remains debated (BOK-21).

Reading in many scripts

Readers of Hindi (an abugida), Chinese (logographic) and English (alphabetic) use slightly different brain strategies. Learning to read in any script changes the brain.

Remember this: Reading is a cultural invention that rewires a natural brain, and it trains us to imagine other minds.

Next: If reading is so powerful, will e-books, audiobooks and AI replace books?

sections.title: Will e-books and AI replace books?
sections.html:
Short answer: Unlikely. They are adding new ways to read, as printing did. E-books, audiobooks and web novels have grown, but printed books still sell strongly worldwide. AI can write text, but books are also about trust, authorship and shared culture, which raises new questions of credit and copyright.

Keywords: future of books, e-books vs print, audiobooks, AI written books, web novels

Every new medium was meant to kill the book

Radio, cinema, television and the internet were each expected to end reading. Instead, books changed shape.

The digital shelf

Michael Hart started Project Gutenberg in 1971, the first digital library. Amazon's Kindle (2007) made e-books mainstream. Audiobooks have grown fast. Web novels and platforms such as Wattpad, China's web-fiction sites and India's Pratilipi (many Indian languages) have created millions of new readers and writers.

AI and the book

AI tools can now draft text, translate and summarise. This raises real questions: who is the author, who gets credited, and was the AI trained on writers' work without permission? Courts and publishers are still deciding. Curious Sparoows labels AI-assisted work openly, which is one honest answer.

What a book still does

A book offers a whole, finished argument or world, by a responsible author, that you can return to. That deep, unbroken attention is hard to replace.

Remember this: The book keeps changing its body: tablet, scroll, codex, screen, voice. It has not lost its soul.

sections.title: Recap: the story of the book in one page
sections.html:
Short answer: Humans told stories in memory, wrote them on clay, leaves and scrolls, printed them, turned them into novels and now read them on screens and hear them as audio. The constant is one mind reaching another.

Keywords: history of books summary, story of literature, books timeline

  1. Memory (forever): oral epics, songs and the Vedas.
  2. Writing (from about 3300 BCE): Sumer, Egypt, China, Mesoamerica.
  3. First authors: Enheduanna, Gilgamesh, Homer, Sangam poets, Valmiki and Vyasa (by tradition).
  4. Leaves, scrolls and codices: palm leaf and birch bark in India, papyrus in Egypt, the codex in Rome.
  5. Paper and print: China (105 CE paper; 868 Diamond Sutra), Korea (1377 Jikji), Gutenberg (about 1455), Goa (1556), Serampore (1800).
  6. The novel: Genji (around 1010), Don Quixote (1605), Durgeshnandini (1865).
  7. Mass reading: cheap paperbacks (Penguin, 1935), libraries and literacy campaigns.
  8. Digital: Project Gutenberg (1971), Kindle (2007), audiobooks, web novels, AI.

Remember this: Every book is a conversation across time; you are the latest person invited.

Next: Start exploring the literatures of the world in Part 1, beginning with India.

parts.title: Literatures of the World
parts.intro:
About this Part. The first great classification is where and in what language a book was written. It begins with India in full depth (classical languages, every Eighth Schedule language, major regional languages, tribal oral literatures and Indian writing in English), then travels continent by continent. Each literature has an identity card (script, oldest works, golden ages, signature forms), its masters, and a Book Register of landmark works. The registers are a curated landmark selection, not a complete list. See "How the registers grow" (BOK-05.6).
Register fields. Year · Title (original, with English meaning) · Author · Form · Awards and adaptations · Why it matters. Dates of ancient works are scholarly estimates. A dash (—) means not recorded here, never a guess. Film adaptations link to the Movies index (MOV-).

sections.title: Indian literatures: one civilisation, many tongues
sections.html:
Before you start — BOK-01. India has 22 languages in the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution, six languages declared "classical" by 2014 (Tamil, Sanskrit, Kannada, Telugu, Malayalam, Odia) and five more added in October 2024 (Marathi, Pali, Prakrit, Assamese, Bengali), and hundreds of mother tongues. Sahitya Akademi recognises 24 languages for its awards (the 22 plus English and Rajasthani). Indian literature is therefore not one literature but a family that shares epics, bhakti poets and modern themes. See also: BOK-12 History of the book, BOK-16.1 Indian awards, MOV-01 Indian cinema (adaptations).

The classical language of ancient India, with literature from the Vedas (from about 1500 BCE) to the present day. Written in many scripts, today mostly Devanagari. Tags: #sanskrit #classical #india

  • Vedic literature: the four Vedas (Rig, Sama, Yajur, Atharva), then Brahmanas, Aranyakas and Upanishads, the philosophical heart of the tradition.
  • Itihasa (the epics): the Ramayana (by tradition Valmiki, the "adi kavi", first poet) and the Mahabharata (by tradition Vyasa), which contains the Bhagavad Gita.
  • Puranas: eighteen major Puranas of myth, genealogy and devotion, such as the Bhagavata Purana.
  • Kavya (court poetry): Ashvaghosha (Buddhacharita), Kalidasa (Raghuvamsha, Kumarasambhava, Meghaduta), Bharavi, Magha, Sriharsha; the five great kavyas (pancha mahakavya).
  • Drama (nataka): Bhasa, Kalidasa (Abhijnanashakuntalam), Shudraka (Mrichchhakatika), Vishakhadatta (Mudrarakshasa), Bhavabhuti (Uttararamacharita).
  • Prose and story: Banabhatta (Kadambari, Harshacharita), Dandin (Dashakumaracharita), the Panchatantra, Hitopadesha, Kathasaritsagara (Somadeva), Vetala Panchavimshati.
  • Lyric and devotion: Bhartrihari's Shatakatraya, Jayadeva's Gita Govinda (12th century), Amaru's Amarushataka.
  • Shastra (knowledge texts): Panini's grammar Ashtadhyayi, Bharata's Natyashastra, Kautilya's Arthashastra, Charaka and Sushruta (medicine), Aryabhata (astronomy), Kalhana's Rajatarangini (history of Kashmir, 1148–49).
  • Modern Sanskrit: writers still publish; Sahitya Akademi gives an annual Sanskrit award.

Languages of early Buddhism and Jainism, declared classical in 2024. Tags: #pali #prakrit #buddhist #jain

  • Pali Canon (Tipitaka): Vinaya, Sutta and Abhidhamma; the Dhammapada and Jataka tales (stories of the Buddha's past lives).
  • Jain Agamas: in Ardhamagadhi Prakrit; later commentaries.
  • Prakrit poetry: Hala's Gaha Sattasai (Maharashtri Prakrit, early centuries CE), seven hundred love poems of village life.
  • Apabhramsha: the bridge to modern North Indian languages; Svayambhu's Ramayana (Paumachariu), Pushpadanta.

India's oldest continuous classical literature after Sanskrit, the first language declared classical (2004). Tags: #tamil #classical #sangam

  • Sangam literature (about 300 BCE–300 CE): the Eight Anthologies (Ettuthokai) and Ten Idylls (Pattuppattu), sorted into akam (love) and puram (war, public life); Tolkappiyam, the oldest grammar.
  • Ethical works: Thiruvalluvar's Thirukkural, 1,330 couplets on virtue, wealth and love, translated into dozens of languages.
  • Twin epics: Silappatikaram (Ilango Adigal) and Manimekalai (Sattanar).
  • Bhakti: the Shaiva Nayanars (Tevaram) and Vaishnava Alvars (Nalayira Divya Prabandham), including Andal, from the 6th–9th centuries.
  • Kamban's Ramavataram (12th century): the great Tamil Ramayana.
  • Modern: Subramania Bharati (poet of freedom), Pudhumaippithan (short story), Kalki (Ponniyin Selvan), Jayakanthan, Sujatha, Ashokamitran, Ambai, Bama (Karukku, Dalit memoir), Perumal Murugan, Imayam, Salma, Vairamuthu.

Classical language (2008); eight Kannada writers have won the Jnanpith Award. Tags: #kannada #classical

  • Early: Kavirajamarga (9th century, earliest surviving work on poetics); Pampa, Ponna and Ranna, the "three gems" of Jain Kannada poetry.
  • Vachana movement (12th century): Basavanna, Akka Mahadevi, Allama Prabhu; short prose poems against caste and ritual.
  • Haridasa songs: Purandara Dasa and Kanaka Dasa.
  • Modern: Kuvempu (first Kannada Jnanpith, 1967), D. R. Bendre, Shivaram Karanth, Masti Venkatesha Iyengar, V. K. Gokak, U. R. Ananthamurthy (Samskara), Girish Karnad (drama), Chandrashekhara Kambara, S. L. Bhyrappa, Devanur Mahadeva, Vivek Shanbhag, Banu Mushtaq (International Booker 2025).

Classical language (2008); famous for its musical verse and avadhanam memory feats. Tags: #telugu #classical

  • Kavitrayam: Nannaya, Tikkana and Errapragada, who rendered the Mahabharata in Telugu (11th–14th centuries).
  • Prabandha age: Krishnadevaraya's court, the Ashtadiggajas; Allasani Peddana; Tenali Ramakrishna of the folk tales.
  • Saints and singers: Vemana (pithy verses), Annamacharya, Tyagaraja (Carnatic songs), Pothana (Bhagavatam).
  • Modern: Gurajada Apparao (Kanyasulkam, 1892 play), Viswanatha Satyanarayana (first Telugu Jnanpith), Sri Sri (Maha Prasthanam), C. Narayana Reddy, Ravuri Bharadwaja, Chalam, Volga.

Classical language (2013) with one of India's highest reading cultures. Tags: #malayalam #classical #kerala

  • Early: Ramacharitam, the Manipravalam style (Malayalam mixed with Sanskrit); Cherusseri's Krishnagatha.
  • Thunchaththu Ezhuthachan (16th century): "father of modern Malayalam", Adhyatma Ramayanam.
  • Modern poets: the triumvirate Kumaran Asan, Ulloor and Vallathol; G. Sankara Kurup (first Jnanpith ever, 1965, for Odakkuzhal).
  • Novel: O. Chandu Menon's Indulekha (1889), Thakazhi Sivasankara Pillai (Chemmeen), Vaikom Muhammad Basheer, S. K. Pottekkatt, M. T. Vasudevan Nair, O. V. Vijayan (Khasakkinte Itihasam), Kamala Das (Madhavikutty), M. Mukundan, Benyamin (Aadujeevitham), K. R. Meera.

The literature of India's most widely spoken language, with roots in Braj, Awadhi and Khari Boli. Tags: #hindi

  • Adikal / Veergatha (about 1000–1350): heroic ballads such as Prithviraj Raso (attributed to Chand Bardai; date debated).
  • Bhakti kal (about 1350–1650): Kabir and the nirgun saints; Surdas (Braj, Krishna); Tulsidas (Ramcharitmanas, Awadhi, 1574 onward); Malik Muhammad Jayasi (Padmavat, 1540); Meera's songs; Raskhan, Rahim.
  • Riti kal (about 1650–1850): ornate court poetry: Keshavdas, Bihari (Satsai), Bhushan, Ghananand.
  • Adhunik kal (modern, from about 1850): Bharatendu Harishchandra, Mahavir Prasad Dwivedi; Chhayavad poets Jaishankar Prasad (Kamayani), Suryakant Tripathi "Nirala", Sumitranandan Pant, Mahadevi Verma.
  • Fiction: Premchand (Godaan, 1936; short stories), Phanishwar Nath Renu (Maila Anchal), Yashpal, Jainendra, Agyeya, Bhisham Sahni (Tamas), Nirmal Verma, Mohan Rakesh, Mannu Bhandari, Krishna Sobti, Shrilal Shukla (Raag Darbari), Manohar Shyam Joshi, Vinod Kumar Shukla, Geetanjali Shree (Ret Samadhi, International Booker 2022 as Tomb of Sand, tr. Daisy Rockwell).
  • Poetry after 1947: Nayi Kavita, Muktibodh, Raghuvir Sahay, Dhumil, Kedarnath Singh, Kunwar Narayan, Harivansh Rai Bachchan (Madhushala), Ramdhari Singh "Dinkar", Dushyant Kumar (Hindi ghazal).
  • Dalit and women's writing: Omprakash Valmiki (Joothan), Mamta Kalia, Maitreyi Pushpa, Chitra Mudgal.

Born in the Deccan and Delhi from Persian, Arabic and Indian roots; the great language of the ghazal. Tags: #urdu #ghazal

  • Dakhni beginnings: Quli Qutb Shah, Wali Dakhni.
  • Classical ghazal: Mir Taqi Mir, Sauda, Ghalib (letters and ghazals), Momin, Zauq, Dagh.
  • Reform and nazm: Hali, Nazir Akbarabadi (poet of everyday life), Muhammad Iqbal, Josh Malihabadi.
  • Progressive Writers' Movement (founded 1936, first conference presided by Premchand): Faiz Ahmad Faiz, Sahir Ludhianvi, Kaifi Azmi, Ali Sardar Jafri, Majrooh Sultanpuri.
  • Fiction: Saadat Hasan Manto (Toba Tek Singh), Ismat Chughtai (Lihaaf), Krishan Chander, Rajinder Singh Bedi, Qurratulain Hyder (Aag ka Darya; Jnanpith 1989), Intizar Husain, Shamsur Rahman Faruqi.
  • Dastangoi: the art of long oral tales such as the Dastan-e Amir Hamza, revived in Delhi from 2005.

Classical language (2024); the first Indian literature to win the Nobel Prize (Tagore, 1913). Tags: #bengali #bangla

  • Charyapada (about 8th–12th centuries): Buddhist songs, the earliest Bengali (and Assamese and Odia) writing.
  • Medieval: Chandidas, Mangal kavya narratives, Krittivas's Ramayana, Chaitanya biographies.
  • Bengal Renaissance: Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar (prose), Michael Madhusudan Dutt (Meghnad Badh Kavya, blank verse), Bankim Chandra (Anandamath with "Vande Mataram").
  • Rabindranath Tagore: Gitanjali, Gora, Ghare Baire, short stories, songs (Rabindrasangeet), two national anthems (India and Bangladesh).
  • After Tagore: Sarat Chandra (Devdas), Kazi Nazrul Islam (the "rebel poet"), Jibanananda Das, Bibhutibhushan Bandyopadhyay (Pather Panchali), Tarashankar, Manik Bandyopadhyay, Mahasweta Devi, Sunil Gangopadhyay, Shirshendu, Satyajit Ray (Feluda), Humayun Ahmed and Taslima Nasrin (Bangladesh).

Classical language (2024); strong traditions of saint poetry, theatre and Dalit autobiography. Tags: #marathi

  • Saints (Varkari tradition): Dnyaneshwar (Dnyaneshwari, 1290), Namdev, Eknath, Tukaram (abhangas), Janabai, Bahinabai.
  • Powada and lavani: heroic ballads and folk song.
  • Modern: Hari Narayan Apte, V. S. Khandekar (Yayati; Jnanpith 1974), Kusumagraj, P. L. Deshpande (humour), Vinda Karandikar, Bhalchandra Nemade (Kosla), Durga Bhagwat, G. A. Kulkarni.
  • Dalit literature: Namdeo Dhasal (Dalit Panthers, 1972), Daya Pawar (Baluta), Laxman Mane, Sharankumar Limbale, Urmila Pawar.
  • Theatre: Vijay Tendulkar (Ghashiram Kotwal), Mahesh Elkunchwar.

Tags: #gujarati

  • Early: Hemachandra's grammar (12th century); Narsinh Mehta (15th century, "Vaishnava Jana To"), Akho, Premanand (akhyana storytelling).
  • Modern: Narmad, Govardhanram Tripathi (Saraswatichandra), Mahatma Gandhi's autobiography (Satya na Prayogo, 1925–29), K. M. Munshi, Umashankar Joshi (Jnanpith 1967, shared), Pannalal Patel, Raghuveer Chaudhari.

Written in Gurmukhi (India) and Shahmukhi (Pakistan). Tags: #punjabi

  • Baba Farid (12th–13th century) and the Guru Granth Sahib (compiled 1604, with verses of the Sikh Gurus and saints of many faiths).
  • Sufi poets: Bulleh Shah, Shah Hussain, Sultan Bahu; Waris Shah's Heer (1766).
  • Modern: Bhai Vir Singh, Amrita Pritam (Pinjar; "Ajj aakhaan Waris Shah nu" on Partition), Shiv Kumar Batalvi, Gurdial Singh, Surjit Patar, Pash.

Classical language (2014). Tags: #odia

  • Sarala Das's Mahabharata (15th century); the Panchasakha saint-poets; Upendra Bhanja (ornate kavya).
  • Modern: Fakir Mohan Senapati (Chha Mana Atha Guntha, 1897, a pioneering realist novel), Gopinath Mohanty (Jnanpith 1973), Sitakant Mahapatra, Pratibha Ray.

Classical language (2024). Tags: #assamese

  • Madhava Kandali's Ramayana (14th century), among the first in a modern Indian language.
  • Srimanta Sankardev (15th–16th century): borgeet songs, ankiya naat plays, the Sattriya tradition.
  • Modern: Lakshminath Bezbarua, Birendra Kumar Bhattacharya (Jnanpith 1979), Mamoni Raisom Goswami (Indira Goswami), Nilmani Phookan.

  • Kashmiri: Lal Ded (Lalleshwari, 14th century vakhs), Habba Khatoon, Mahjoor, Rahman Rahi (Jnanpith 2004).
  • Konkani: Shenoy Goembab, Ravindra Kelekar (Jnanpith 2006), Damodar Mauzo (Jnanpith 2022).
  • Maithili: Vidyapati (14th–15th century love songs), Harimohan Jha, Nagarjuna (Yatri).
  • Manipuri (Meiteilon): the Cheitharol Kumbaba royal chronicle, Hijam Anganghal, Lamabam Kamal.
  • Nepali: Bhanubhakta Acharya (Nepali Ramayana), Laxmi Prasad Devkota (Muna Madan), Indra Bahadur Rai (Darjeeling).
  • Sindhi: Shah Abdul Latif Bhittai (Shah Jo Risalo), Sachal Sarmast; writers in India after Partition such as Moti Prakash.
  • Santali: written in the Ol Chiki script created by Pandit Raghunath Murmu (1925); oral creation stories.
  • Dogri: Padma Sachdev, Dinoo Bhai Pant.
  • Bodo: hymns, folk literature and modern poetry in the Devanagari script.

  • Rajasthani (recognised by Sahitya Akademi): Dingal and Pingal bardic poetry, Dhola Maru, Meera's songs, Veli Krishan Rukmani ri (Prithviraj Rathore), Vijaydan Detha ("Bijji", folk tales, Duvidha), Kanhaiyalal Sethia, Chandra Prakash Deval.
  • Bhojpuri: Bhikhari Thakur (Bidesiya, "the Shakespeare of Bhojpuri"), folk songs of migration.
  • Awadhi and Braj: the bhakti classics of Tulsidas and Surdas.
  • Tulu, Kodava, Garhwali, Kumaoni, Chhattisgarhi, Haryanvi and others: oral epics, songs and modern writing.

  • Creation myths, songs and epics of the Gond (Pandvani-style performances), Bhil (Bhilodi Mahabharata), Santal, Munda, Oraon, Khasi, Mizo, Naga and Toda peoples.
  • Collectors and champions: Verrier Elwin, Ganesh Devy (People's Linguistic Survey of India, Bhasha Research Centre), Ramnika Gupta.
  • Modern Adivasi writers: Hansda Sowvendra Shekhar, Temsula Ao, Mamang Dai, Jacinta Kerketta, Narayan (Malayalam, Kocharethi).

  • Pioneers: Henry Derozio, Toru Dutt, Bankim's Rajmohan's Wife (1864), Sarojini Naidu, Sri Aurobindo (Savitri), Tagore's own translations.
  • The founding trio: Mulk Raj Anand (Untouchable, 1935), R. K. Narayan (Malgudi), Raja Rao (Kanthapura, 1938).
  • Midnight's children: Salman Rushdie (Midnight's Children, Booker 1981), Vikram Seth (A Suitable Boy), Amitav Ghosh (Jnanpith 2018, first English-language writer to win it), Arundhati Roy (The God of Small Things, Booker 1997), Anita Desai, Kiran Desai (Booker 2006), Rohinton Mistry, Upamanyu Chatterjee, Aravind Adiga (Booker 2008), Jhumpa Lahiri (Pulitzer 2000).
  • Poets: Nissim Ezekiel, A. K. Ramanujan, Kamala Das, Dom Moraes, Jayanta Mahapatra, Arun Kolatkar (Jejuri), Eunice de Souza, Jeet Thayil.
  • Popular fiction: Ruskin Bond, Chetan Bhagat, Amish Tripathi, Anuja Chauhan, Ashwin Sanghi.
  • Translation as Indian literature: A. K. Ramanujan, Arshia Sattar, Daisy Rockwell, Deepa Bhasthi, Arunava Sinha and others make the bhasha literatures available across India and the world.

sections.title: Literatures of Asia
sections.html:
Before you start — BOK-02. Asia holds the oldest written literatures after Mesopotamia and Egypt, and several of the world's great classical traditions: Chinese, Persian, Arabic, Japanese. Many share forms across borders: the ghazal travelled from Arabic to Persian, Urdu and now English; the Ramayana travelled across South-East Asia. See also: BOK-01 India, BOK-06 Poetry forms, MOV-04 Asian cinema.

  • Classics: the Shijing (Classic of Poetry), Confucius's Analects, the Daodejing (attributed to Laozi), Zhuangzi, Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian (about 94 BCE).
  • Tang poetry (618–907): Li Bai, Du Fu, Wang Wei, Bai Juyi, the golden age of Chinese verse; Song ci lyrics (Su Shi, Li Qingzhao).
  • The Four Great Classical Novels: Romance of the Three Kingdoms, Water Margin, Journey to the West (Wu Cheng'en; the Monkey King, based on the monk Xuanzang's real journey to India) and Dream of the Red Chamber (Cao Xueqin, 18th century).
  • Modern: Lu Xun ("A Madman's Diary", 1918; The True Story of Ah Q), Lao She, Ba Jin, Eileen Chang, Mo Yan (Nobel 2012), Gao Xingjian (Nobel 2000, French citizen), Yu Hua, Can Xue, Liu Cixin (The Three-Body Problem; Hugo Award 2015), Jin Yong (wuxia novels).

  • Classical: the Kojiki (712) and Man'yōshū poetry anthology (8th century); Murasaki Shikibu's The Tale of Genji (about 1010); Sei Shōnagon's The Pillow Book; The Tale of the Heike.
  • Forms: waka and tanka, renga, haiku (Matsuo Bashō, Buson, Issa, Shiki), noh and kabuki drama, Chikamatsu's puppet plays.
  • Modern: Natsume Sōseki (Kokoro), Ryūnosuke Akutagawa ("Rashōmon"), Yasunari Kawabata (Nobel 1968), Yukio Mishima, Kenzaburō Ōe (Nobel 1994), Haruki Murakami, Banana Yoshimoto, Yoko Ogawa, Sayaka Murata, Kazuo Ishiguro (British, born in Japan; Nobel 2017).
  • Manga and light novels: see BOK-10.9.

  • Classical: hyangga and sijo poetry; the Samguk yusa; The Tale of Chunhyang (pansori story); the Hangul alphabet created under King Sejong (promulgated 1446) made literacy easy.
  • Modern: Yi Sang, Pak Kyongni (Land), Ko Un, Shin Kyung-sook (Please Look After Mom), Han Kang (The Vegetarian, International Booker 2016 with translator Deborah Smith; Nobel Prize 2024, the first Korean and first Asian woman laureate), Cho Nam-joo (Kim Jiyoung, Born 1982), webtoons.

  • Epic: Ferdowsi's Shahnameh (completed 1010), the national epic of Iran, about 50,000 couplets.
  • Mystical and lyric masters: Rumi (Masnavi), Hafez (ghazals; consulted for omens in Iranian homes), Saadi (Gulistan, Bustan), Attar (The Conference of the Birds), Omar Khayyam (Rubaiyat, made famous in English by Edward FitzGerald, 1859), Nizami (Layla and Majnun).
  • India's Persian: Amir Khusrau, Bedil, Ghalib's Persian works; Persian was a court language of India for centuries.
  • Modern: Sadegh Hedayat (The Blind Owl), Forugh Farrokhzad, Simin Daneshvar, Shahrnush Parsipur.

  • Pre-Islamic poetry: the Mu'allaqat (the "hanging odes"), qasida form.
  • The Qur'an (7th century) as the supreme model of Arabic prose and rhyme (see BOK-11).
  • Classical: al-Mutanabbi, Abu Nuwas, al-Jahiz; the Maqamat of al-Hariri; One Thousand and One Nights (stories gathered from Indian, Persian and Arab sources; Scheherazade); Ibn Battuta's travels; Ibn Khaldun's Muqaddimah (1377).
  • Andalusia: Ibn Hazm (The Ring of the Dove), Ibn Arabi, Ibn Rushd.
  • Modern (Nahda and after): Naguib Mahfouz (Cairo Trilogy; Nobel 1988), Taha Hussein, Mahmoud Darwish, Nizar Qabbani, Adonis, Tayeb Salih (Season of Migration to the North), Ghassan Kanafani, Jokha Alharthi (Celestial Bodies, International Booker 2019).

  • Turkic epics: the Book of Dede Korkut; Manas (Kyrgyz, one of the longest epics); Yunus Emre's Sufi poems.
  • Ottoman divan poetry: Fuzuli, Baki, Nedim.
  • Modern Turkish: Nazım Hikmet, Yaşar Kemal (Memed, My Hawk), Orhan Pamuk (Nobel 2006; My Name Is Red), Elif Şafak.
  • Central Asia: Alisher Navoi (Chagatai), Chinghiz Aitmatov (Kyrgyz).

  • Pakistan: Faiz, Manto, Intizar Husain, Bapsi Sidhwa, Mohammed Hanif, Kamila Shamsie (Women's Prize 2018).
  • Bangladesh: Kazi Nazrul Islam (national poet), Jasimuddin, Humayun Ahmed, Selina Hossain.
  • Sri Lanka: Sinhala classics; Martin Wickramasinghe; Michael Ondaatje (The English Patient, Booker 1992), Shehan Karunatilaka (Booker 2022).
  • Nepal: Bhanubhakta, Devkota, Parijat.
  • Myanmar, Thailand, Cambodia, Laos: Ramayana retellings (Thai Ramakien, Khmer Reamker), Thai poet Sunthorn Phu.
  • Indonesia and Malaysia: wayang stories, Hikayat, Pramoedya Ananta Toer (Buru Quartet), Chairil Anwar, Eka Kurniawan.
  • Vietnam: Nguyễn Du's The Tale of Kiều (national poem), Bảo Ninh (The Sorrow of War).
  • Philippines: José Rizal (Noli Me Tángere, 1887), Nick Joaquín, F. Sionil José.

  • The Hebrew Bible (Tanakh; see BOK-11), Talmud, medieval poets (Yehuda Halevi), Yiddish literature (Sholem Aleichem, Isaac Bashevis Singer, Nobel 1978), modern Hebrew (S. Y. Agnon, Nobel 1966; Amos Oz; David Grossman, International Booker 2017).

sections.title: Literatures of Europe
sections.html:
Before you start — BOK-03. Europe's literatures grew from Greek and Latin roots, the Bible, medieval epics and the printing press. National literatures rose with national languages from the 1300s. See also: BOK-13 Literary movements, MOV-03 European cinema.

  • Greek: Homer (Iliad, Odyssey), Hesiod, Sappho (lyric), Aesop (fables), the tragedians Aeschylus, Sophocles (Oedipus the King) and Euripides, the comic Aristophanes, historians Herodotus and Thucydides, philosophers Plato and Aristotle (Poetics).
  • Latin: Virgil (Aeneid), Ovid (Metamorphoses), Horace, Catullus, Cicero, Seneca, Augustine (Confessions).

  • Old and Middle English: Beowulf, Chaucer (The Canterbury Tales, about 1387–1400), Sir Gawain and the Green Knight.
  • Renaissance: Shakespeare (37 to 39 plays and 154 sonnets), Marlowe, Spenser, Donne, the King James Bible (1611), Milton (Paradise Lost, 1667).
  • 18th century and the rise of the novel: Defoe (Robinson Crusoe, 1719), Swift (Gulliver's Travels), Richardson, Fielding, Samuel Johnson's Dictionary (1755).
  • Romantics: Blake, Wordsworth, Coleridge, Byron, Shelley, Keats, Mary Shelley (Frankenstein, 1818).
  • Victorians: Jane Austen (just before, 1811–1817), the Brontës, Dickens, George Eliot (Middlemarch), Thomas Hardy, Lewis Carroll, Tennyson, Browning.
  • Modernists and after: Joseph Conrad, Virginia Woolf, James Joyce (Ulysses, 1922), T. S. Eliot, W. B. Yeats (Nobel 1923), George Orwell, Samuel Beckett (Nobel 1969), Doris Lessing, Seamus Heaney, Hilary Mantel, Zadie Smith, Sally Rooney.

  • The Song of Roland; Rabelais; Montaigne (invented the essay, 1580); Molière, Racine, Corneille; Voltaire (Candide), Rousseau; Victor Hugo (Les Misérables), Balzac, Flaubert (Madame Bovary), Zola, Baudelaire (Les Fleurs du mal), Rimbaud; Proust (In Search of Lost Time), Colette; Sartre, Camus (The Stranger), Simone de Beauvoir; the nouveau roman; Annie Ernaux (Nobel 2022); Francophone writers from Africa, the Caribbean and Quebec.

  • Nibelungenlied; Luther's Bible; Goethe (Faust), Schiller; the Brothers Grimm (folk tales, 1812); Heine; Thomas Mann (Buddenbrooks; Nobel 1929), Rilke, Kafka (The Metamorphosis), Hermann Hesse (Siddhartha, 1922; Nobel 1946), Brecht, Günter Grass, W. G. Sebald, Herta Müller, Jenny Erpenbeck (International Booker 2024).

  • Pushkin (Eugene Onegin), Gogol, Lermontov; the great novelists Tolstoy (War and Peace, Anna Karenina) and Dostoevsky (Crime and Punishment, The Brothers Karamazov); Turgenev; Chekhov (stories and plays); Gorky; Akhmatova, Tsvetaeva, Mandelstam, Pasternak (Doctor Zhivago; Nobel 1958), Bulgakov (The Master and Margarita), Solzhenitsyn (Nobel 1970), Nabokov.

sections.title: Literatures of Africa and Oceania
sections.html:
Before you start — BOK-05. Africa has the world's richest living oral literatures and some of the oldest written ones (Egyptian, Ge'ez in Ethiopia, Swahili in Arabic script, the Timbuktu manuscripts). Modern African literature is written in English, French, Portuguese, Arabic and African languages (Yoruba, Gikuyu, Swahili, Zulu, Amharic). Oceania includes Aboriginal Australian, Māori and Pacific traditions. See also: MOV-05 Africa and Oceania.

  • Egyptian Book of the Dead, The Tale of Sinuhe, love songs; the Ethiopian Kebra Nagast (14th century, Ge'ez).

  • Oral epics: Sundiata (Mali), the griot tradition, Yoruba ifá poetry.
  • Timbuktu manuscripts: hundreds of thousands of Arabic and Ajami manuscripts on law, astronomy and poetry.
  • Modern: Chinua Achebe (Things Fall Apart, 1958), Wole Soyinka (Nobel 1986, first African laureate), Amos Tutuola, Buchi Emecheta, Ben Okri (Booker 1991), Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie, Ama Ata Aidoo (Ghana), Léopold Sédar Senghor and Mariama Bâ (Senegal), Ahmadou Kourouma.

M. Coetzee (Booker 1983 and 1999; Nobel 2003), Damon Galgut (Booker 2021), Alan Paton (Cry, the Beloved Country), Zakes Mda; Gandhi's Indian Opinion newspaper and Hind Swaraj (1909) were written in South Africa.

parts.title: Kinds of Literature: Forms and Genres
parts.intro: About this Part. The second great classification is what kind of writing a book is. Literature has two great trunks, poetry and prose, plus drama and the oral tradition, which mix both. Prose divides into fiction and non-fiction, and fiction into many genres. Sacred texts are a category of their own. Each entry gives a one- or two-line definition and examples from India and the world. Indian poetics (kavya, rasa, dhvani) is covered in Part 6 (BOK-20).

sections.title: Poetry: the first trunk
sections.html:
Before you start — BOK-06. Poetry is language shaped by rhythm, sound and image, usually in lines. Forms are like containers: a sonnet has fourteen lines, a haiku three, a doha two. Learning a few forms helps you hear poems better. See also: MUS (songs and lyrics), BOK-20 Literary theory.

  • Epic (mahakavya): a long story of heroes, gods and nations in elevated verse; Mahabharata, Ramayana, Iliad, Shahnameh, Silappatikaram, Paradise Lost.
  • Mock epic: epic style for trivial things; Pope's The Rape of the Lock.
  • Ballad: a short sung story in simple stanzas; English and Scottish ballads, Rajasthani and Punjabi folk ballads (Heer Ranjha).
  • Verse novel: a novel in verse; Pushkin's Eugene Onegin, Vikram Seth's The Golden Gate (1986).
  • Akhyana and kathakavya: Indian narrative poems sung by storytellers; Premanand's Gujarati akhyanas.

  • Lyric: a short poem of personal feeling, originally sung to the lyre; Sappho, Mirabai, Keats.
  • Ode: a formal poem of praise or reflection; Pindar, Keats's "Ode to a Nightingale".
  • Elegy and marsiya: poems of mourning; Gray's "Elegy", Urdu marsiya on Karbala (Mir Anis, Mirza Dabeer).
  • Pastoral: idealised country life; Theocritus, Virgil's Eclogues.
  • Pada and bhajan: devotional songs of the bhakti saints (Surdas, Meera, Tukaram's abhangas).

  • Sonnet: fourteen lines; Petrarchan (8 + 6) and Shakespearean (4 + 4 + 4 + 2).
  • Villanelle: nineteen lines with two repeating refrains; Dylan Thomas's "Do not go gentle".
  • Terza rima: interlocking three-line stanzas; Dante.
  • Blank verse: unrhymed iambic pentameter; Shakespeare, Milton; brought into Bengali by Michael Madhusudan Dutt (amitrakshar chhanda).
  • Limerick: five comic lines; Edward Lear.

  • Ghazal: rhyming couplets (sher), each complete in itself, with a repeated refrain (radif) and rhyme (qafiya), the poet's pen name (takhallus) in the last couplet (maqta); Hafez, Mir, Ghalib, Faiz; now written in Hindi, English and other languages.
  • Qasida: a long ode of praise.
  • Masnavi: rhyming couplets for long narratives; Rumi.
  • Rubai: a four-line quatrain (AABA); Omar Khayyam.
  • Nazm: Urdu poem on a single theme, freer than the ghazal; Iqbal, Faiz.
  • Qawwali and kafi: Sufi poems for singing; Amir Khusrau, Bulleh Shah.

  • Shloka (anushtubh): Sanskrit couplet of 32 syllables, the metre of the epics.
  • Doha: two-line Hindi couplet (13 + 11 matras per half); Kabir, Rahim, Bihari.
  • Chaupai: four-part metre used with dohas in the Ramcharitmanas and the Hanuman Chalisa.
  • Soratha, kavitt, savaiya, chhappay: other Hindi metres of the riti and bhakti poets.
  • Venba and kural: Tamil metres; the Thirukkural couplet.
  • Vachana: Kannada free prose-poem of the 12th century.
  • Abhanga and ovi: Marathi devotional metres.
  • Vakh and shruk: Kashmiri mystic verses of Lal Ded and Nund Rishi.
  • Shayari and mushaira: the culture of reciting couplets at public poetry gatherings; kavi sammelan in Hindi.

  • Haiku: Japanese three-phrase poem (5–7–5 sounds) with a season word (kigo); Bashō.
  • Tanka and waka: five-line Japanese poem (5–7–5–7–7).
  • Renga: linked verse written by several poets in turn.
  • Sijo: Korean three-line poem.
  • Shi and ci: Chinese regulated verse and song lyrics.

  • Free verse: no fixed metre or rhyme; Whitman, Nirala's mukt chhand, Nayi Kavita.
  • Prose poem: poetry in paragraphs; Baudelaire, Tagore's later work.
  • Concrete and visual poetry: shape on the page as meaning.
  • Spoken word and slam: poetry for performance; India's open-mic scene.
  • Song lyrics and rap: Bob Dylan's Nobel (2016); Gulzar, Javed Akhtar and Sahir in film (MUS).
  • Instapoetry: short poems shared on social media; Rupi Kaur.

sections.title: Prose fiction: the forms of storytelling
sections.html:
Before you start — BOK-07. Fiction is invented narrative in prose. Its forms are mainly sorted by length. Word counts are common publishing guides (for example, those used by the Hugo and Nebula awards), not strict laws. See also: BOK-10 Genre fiction, BOK-18 The craft of writing.

  • Novel: a long prose fiction, usually over 40,000 words; room for many characters and years.
  • Novella: 17,500 to 40,000 words (Hugo/Nebula guide); Kafka's The Metamorphosis, Hemingway's The Old Man and the Sea.
  • Novelette: 7,500 to 17,500 words.
  • Short story: readable in one sitting; Chekhov, Premchand, Manto, Munro, O. Henry, Maupassant.
  • Flash fiction and micro-fiction: under about 1,000 words; the six-word story.
  • Fable, parable and fairy tale: short moral or magical tales; Aesop, Panchatantra, Jataka, Grimm, Andersen.
  • Frame story: stories inside a story; Arabian Nights, Panchatantra, Decameron, Kathasaritsagara.

  • Epistolary: told in letters; Dracula, Frankenstein in part.
  • Bildungsroman: the growing-up novel; Great Expectations, Pather Panchali.
  • Picaresque: adventures of a rogue on the road; Lazarillo de Tormes.
  • Historical novel: fiction set in a real past; Walter Scott, Ponniyin Selvan, Mantel's Wolf Hall.
  • Saga and roman-fleuve: a long family or multi-volume story; Buddenbrooks, The Forsyte Saga.
  • Stream of consciousness: following thoughts as they flow; Woolf, Joyce.
  • Metafiction: fiction aware of being fiction; Calvino's If on a winter's night a traveler.
  • Anchalik (regional) novel: Hindi novels rooted in one region's dialect and life; Renu's Maila Anchal.
  • Partition literature: stories of 1947; Manto, Bhisham Sahni, Amrita Pritam, Khushwant Singh's Train to Pakistan.

  • Realism: life as it is; Premchand, Tolstoy, George Eliot.
  • Naturalism: people shaped by heredity and environment; Zola.
  • Magical realism: magic told as normal; García Márquez, Rushdie.
  • Satire: ridicule to expose folly; Swift, Shrilal Shukla, Harishankar Parsai (vyangya).
  • Allegory: story with a second, symbolic meaning; Bunyan, Orwell's Animal Farm.
  • Absurdism: life without meaning shown through strangeness; Kafka, Camus, Beckett.

sections.title: Non-fiction: true stories and ideas
sections.html:
Before you start — BOK-08. Non-fiction claims to be true. Its value depends on evidence, honesty and clear writing. Many of the best-selling books in India are non-fiction: exam guides, biographies and self-help. See also: Curriculum Index (subject books), BOK-17 Best-sellers.

  • Biography: a life written by someone else; Boswell's Life of Johnson, Rajmohan Gandhi's lives of Gandhi and Patel.
  • Autobiography: one's own life; Gandhi's The Story of My Experiments with Truth, Nehru's An Autobiography, Ambedkar's Waiting for a Visa, A. P. J. Abdul Kalam's Wings of Fire.
  • Memoir: a part of one's life or one theme; Maya Angelou, Michelle Obama's Becoming, Mamta Kalia's Jeete Jee Allahabad (Sahitya Akademi 2025).
  • Diary and letters: Anne Frank's diary; Nehru's Letters from a Father to His Daughter; Ghalib's letters.
  • Charita and tazkira: Indian royal biographies (Harshacharita) and Persian biographical dictionaries of poets; the Mughal memoirs Baburnama and Jahangir's Tuzuk.

  • Essay: a short exploration of one idea; Montaigne invented the word ("attempt"); Bacon, Orwell, Hazari Prasad Dwivedi, Ramachandra Shukla (Hindi nibandh).
  • Philosophy: Plato's dialogues, the Upanishads, Confucius, Kant, Simone de Beauvoir, Ambedkar's Annihilation of Caste (1936).
  • History: Herodotus, Sima Qian, Kalhana, Ibn Khaldun, Abul Fazl's Akbarnama, Romila Thapar, Ramachandra Guha (India after Gandhi), William Dalrymple.
  • Popular science: Darwin's On the Origin of Species (1859), Carl Sagan's Cosmos, Stephen Hawking's A Brief History of Time, Richard Dawkins, Siddhartha Mukherjee (The Emperor of All Maladies, Pulitzer 2011), Jayant Narlikar.
  • Politics and economics: Kautilya's Arthashastra, Machiavelli's The Prince, Adam Smith, Marx and Engels, Amartya Sen (The Argumentative Indian), Thomas Piketty.
  • Self-help and personal development: Dale Carnegie, Stephen Covey, James Clear's Atomic Habits; read with a critical eye.

  • Travel writing: Xuanzang, Ibn Battuta, Marco Polo, Al-Biruni's Kitab al-Hind (about 1030), Rahul Sankrityayan ("father of Hindi travel writing"), Pico Iyer.
  • Journalism and reportage: P. Sainath's Everybody Loves a Good Drought, Katherine Boo's Behind the Beautiful Forevers, Svetlana Alexievich (Nobel 2015, oral history).
  • True crime: Truman Capote's In Cold Blood.
  • Nature writing: Gilbert White, Rachel Carson's Silent Spring (1962, launched modern environmentalism), Salim Ali's The Book of Indian Birds, Jim Corbett.
  • Reference books: dictionaries, encyclopedias (Diderot's Encyclopédie, Britannica since 1768, Wikipedia since 2001), atlases, almanacs, panchangs.
  • How-to, cookbooks and craft books: links to COK, GRD, CRO, KNT, EMB and SEW indexes.
  • Textbooks and exam guides: NCERT books, competitive-exam guides (links to the Curriculum Index and Exam Guide).

sections.title: Drama and the oral tradition
sections.html:
Before you start — BOK-09. Drama is literature written to be performed, and oral literature is literature that lives in performance. Both are often missed when people think "books". See also: MOV-18 (rasa in cinema), MUS.

  • Sanskrit nataka and prakarana: heroic and social plays; Kalidasa, Shudraka; rules in the Natyashastra.
  • Greek tragedy and comedy: the origin of Western drama.
  • Noh, kabuki and Chinese opera: East Asian theatre forms.
  • Shakespearean and Elizabethan drama.
  • Modern realist drama: Ibsen, Chekhov, Arthur Miller, Tennessee Williams.
  • Theatre of the Absurd: Beckett (Waiting for Godot), Ionesco.
  • Modern Indian theatre: Tagore, Mohan Rakesh (Ashadh Ka Ek Din), Vijay Tendulkar, Badal Sircar (Third Theatre), Girish Karnad (Tughlaq, Hayavadana), Habib Tanvir (Charandas Chor), Safdar Hashmi (street theatre).
  • Folk drama: Yakshagana, Jatra, Tamasha, Nautanki, Khyal (Rajasthan), Bhavai, Terukkuttu, Ramlila.

  • Oral epics: Pabuji, Devnarayan, Alha-Udal, the Manas, Sundiata.
  • Folk tales: collected by the Grimms, Verrier Elwin, A. K. Ramanujan (Folktales from India, 1991), Vijaydan Detha.
  • Proverbs, riddles and lullabies: the smallest literature, and among the oldest.
  • Myth: sacred stories of origins (see BOK-11 and BOK-20.4).
  • Urban legends and internet folklore: new oral literature online.

sections.title: Genre fiction: the shelves of the bookshop
sections.html:
Before you start — BOK-10. Genres are families of stories with shared expectations: a mystery promises a solution, a romance promises love at the centre. "Literary fiction" is itself sometimes treated as a genre. Genres mix freely. See also: MOV-06 Film genres (many films adapt genre books).

A crime, an investigation and a solution. Poe's Dupin (1841), Wilkie Collins's The Moonstone (1868), Arthur Conan Doyle's Sherlock Holmes (1887), Agatha Christie, Georges Simenon; India's Byomkesh Bakshi (Sharadindu Bandyopadhyay), Feluda (Satyajit Ray), Ibn-e-Safi's Urdu spy novels, Surender Mohan Pathak, Hindi "pulp" (lugdi) novels.

  • Sub-genres: cozy, hard-boiled (Chandler, Hammett), police procedural, Nordic noir, legal thriller, locked-room mystery, historical mystery.

Danger and a race against time. John Buchan, Ian Fleming (James Bond), John le Carré (espionage), Frederick Forsyth, Dan Brown, Lee Child; India's Ashwin Sanghi, Mukul Deva. Sub-genres: spy, techno-thriller, psychological thriller, political thriller.

A central love story with an emotionally satisfying ending. Jane Austen as ancestor; Mills & Boon (1908) and Harlequin; Nora Roberts, Colleen Hoover; India's Anuja Chauhan, Durjoy Datta and Hindi and Urdu romances. Sub-genres: historical, contemporary, romantic comedy, paranormal, "romantasy".

Magic and invented worlds. Roots in myth and epic; George MacDonald, Tolkien (The Lord of the Rings), C. S. Lewis, Ursula K. Le Guin, Terry Pratchett, J. K. Rowling, George R. R. Martin, N. K. Jemisin (three Hugos in a row, 2016–2018); Indian mythological fantasy: Amish's Shiva Trilogy, Samit Basu, Anand Neelakantan. Sub-genres: high/epic, urban, sword and sorcery, mythic, grimdark, portal fantasy.

Stories driven by science, technology and "what if". Mary Shelley, Jules Verne, H. G. Wells, Asimov, Arthur C. Clarke, Philip K. Dick, Octavia Butler, Liu Cixin; India's Jagadish Chandra Bose (Niruddesher Kahini, 1896), Begum Rokeya Sakhawat Hossain (Sultana's Dream, 1905, feminist utopia), Satyajit Ray's Professor Shonku, Jayant Narlikar, Vandana Singh. Sub-genres: hard SF, space opera, cyberpunk, dystopia, climate fiction (cli-fi), solarpunk, afrofuturism.

Fear, the uncanny and the supernatural. Horace Walpole (The Castle of Otranto, 1764), Bram Stoker (Dracula, 1897), H. P. Lovecraft, Stephen King, Shirley Jackson; Indian ghost stories (bhoot katha), Ruskin Bond's ghost tales, Rabindranath's "Kshudhita Pashan" (The Hungry Stones).

Swashbucklers, quests and the past re-imagined. Dumas (The Three Musketeers), Stevenson (Treasure Island), Kalki's Ponniyin Selvan, Devaki Nandan Khatri's Chandrakanta (1888, a Hindi bestseller that made people learn Hindi to read it).

  • Picture books: Eric Carle, Maurice Sendak; Tulika and Pratham Books in India.
  • Children's classics: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, The Jungle Book (Kipling, set in India), Pinocchio, Enid Blyton, Roald Dahl, Panchatantra retold, Amar Chitra Katha (1967, Anant Pai), Chandamama (1947), Champak, Tinkle.
  • Young adult: S. E. Hinton's The Outsiders (1967) as an early landmark; Harry Potter, The Hunger Games; Paro Anand.
  • Award: Hans Christian Andersen Award, Newbery and Carnegie medals, Sahitya Akademi Bal Sahitya Puraskar.

  • Comics: comic strips and books; Tintin (Hergé), Asterix, Marvel and DC superheroes; India's Amar Chitra Katha, Chacha Chaudhary (Pran, 1971), Raj Comics, Diamond Comics.
  • Graphic novel: long-form comics; Art Spiegelman's Maus (Pulitzer special citation 1992), Marjane Satrapi's Persepolis; Sarnath Banerjee's Corridor (2004, often called India's first graphic novel), Orijit Sen's River of Stories (1994).
  • Manga and manhwa: Japanese and Korean comics; Osamu Tezuka ("god of manga"), One Piece, webtoons.

  • Literary fiction: focused on style, character and ideas more than plot; most Booker winners.
  • Speculative fiction: umbrella term for SF, fantasy and horror.
  • Western, sea story, war novel, campus novel, sports fiction (SPT), food fiction (COK).
  • Fan fiction and web novels: readers writing in others' worlds; Wattpad, Archive of Our Own (Hugo Award 2019 for Best Related Work), Pratilipi in Indian languages.

sections.title: Sacred and scriptural texts
sections.html:
Before you start — BOK-11. Sacred texts are some of the oldest, most read and most translated books in the world. This index lists them as literature and as cultural heritage, respectfully and without ranking faiths. Each tradition's own understanding of its texts comes first. See also: BOK-21 Literature and society.

  • Hindu: shruti (the Vedas and Upanishads) and smriti (epics, Puranas, Dharmashastras, Agamas); the Bhagavad Gita.
  • Buddhist: the Pali Tipitaka, Mahayana sutras (such as the Lotus Sutra, Heart Sutra), the Tibetan Kangyur and Tengyur.
  • Jain: Agamas; Umaswati's Tattvartha Sutra; the Kalpa Sutra.
  • Sikh: Sri Guru Granth Sahib (compiled 1604, installed as eternal Guru in 1708), with verses of six Gurus and fifteen bhagats including Kabir, Namdev, Ravidas and Farid.

  • Jewish: the Tanakh (Torah, Prophets, Writings) and Talmud.
  • Christian: the Bible (Old and New Testaments); the most printed and translated book in history (full Bible in over 700 languages, according to Wycliffe Global Alliance).
  • Islamic: the Qur'an (revealed in Arabic in the 7th century) and the Hadith collections.
  • Zoroastrian / Parsi: the Avesta, including the Gathas of Zarathustra.
  • Bahá'í: the Kitáb-i-Aqdas.

  • Chinese: the Confucian classics and the Daodejing; the I Ching.
  • Japanese Shinto: Kojiki and Nihon Shoki.
  • Indigenous sacred narratives: the Popol Vuh, Aboriginal Dreaming stories, African creation myths.

parts.title: History: the Story of the Book and of Literature
parts.intro: About this Part. The book's history is told twice. First as material history (what people wrote on and how copies were made), then as literary history (the movements and ages of writing). The intro twig in Part 0 is the two-minute version; this is the full map. Dates for ancient events are scholarly estimates.

sections.title: Timeline of the book: from memory to machine
sections.html:
Before you start — BOK-12. Every age changed the body of the book: what it was made of, who could copy it and who could read it. Follow India and the world side by side. See also: TEC (printing, paper and digital technology), BOK-19 Publishing.

  • Oral literature everywhere: myths, songs and law kept in memory; cave art and symbols as early storytelling.
  • Vedic oral transmission in India from about 1500 BCE, still alive today.

  • Cuneiform on clay (Sumer, about 3300–3100 BCE); the library of Ashurbanipal (7th century BCE).
  • Hieroglyphs and papyrus (Egypt, from about 3200 BCE).
  • Indus script (about 2600–1900 BCE): undeciphered seals.
  • Chinese oracle-bone script (about 1200 BCE), ancestor of today's characters.
  • The alphabet: Proto-Sinaitic and Phoenician scripts (about 1900–1050 BCE), parent of Greek, Latin, Arabic and Hebrew; Aramaic influenced Kharosthi.

  • Brahmi in the edicts of Ashoka (3rd century BCE), parent of almost all Indian and South-East Asian scripts; Kharosthi in the north-west.
  • Tamil-Brahmi cave inscriptions (from about the 3rd–2nd century BCE).
  • Palm leaf and birch bark manuscripts; copper-plate grants; Jain bhandars; the Gilgit and Bakhshali manuscripts.
  • Great libraries: Nalanda (5th–12th century) with its library called Dharmaganja; Vikramashila; Mughal imperial library; Saraswati Mahal Library, Thanjavur (one of Asia's oldest surviving libraries); Khuda Bakhsh Library, Patna (1891); Raza Library, Rampur.
  • Illustrated manuscripts: Jain Kalpa Sutra paintings, Mughal Hamzanama and Razmnama (Persian Mahabharata), Rajput and Pahari painted Gita Govindas.

  • Codex: bound pages, spreading in the Roman world from the 1st century CE and favoured by early Christians.
  • Paper invented in China (traditionally Cai Lun, 105 CE); spread to Samarkand (751), Baghdad (about 794), Spain and later Europe.
  • Monastic scriptoria and illuminated manuscripts (the Book of Kells, about 800).
  • The Islamic book: Baghdad's House of Wisdom, calligraphy, bookbinding, paper mills; Timbuktu manuscripts.

  • Woodblock printing in China; the Diamond Sutra (868, oldest dated printed book).
  • Movable type: Bi Sheng (clay, about 1040); Korea's Jikji (metal, 1377).
  • Gutenberg (Mainz, about 1450; 42-line Bible about 1455); the "incunabula" (books printed before 1501).
  • Printing in India: Goa (1556), the Tamil Thambiran Vanakkam (1578), Danish missionaries at Tranquebar (1712; Ziegenbalg's Tamil Bible), Calcutta presses (1777 onward), Serampore Mission Press (1800), Fort William College (1800) and its Hindi and Urdu prose books.
  • Newspapers: Hicky's Bengal Gazette (1780), Samachar Darpan (Bengali, 1818), Udant Martand (first Hindi newspaper, 30 May 1826, now Hindi Journalism Day), Jam-e-Jahan-Numa (Urdu/Persian, 1822).

  • Steam presses and cheap paper: books and magazines for everyone; serialised novels (Dickens).
  • Lithography made printing Urdu nastaliq and Indian scripts easy; Nawal Kishore Press, Lucknow (1858), printed thousands of titles in Urdu, Hindi, Persian, Sanskrit and Arabic.
  • Copyright laws: Statute of Anne (Britain, 1710); Berne Convention (1886); India's Copyright Act (1957).
  • Public libraries: Andrew Carnegie's libraries; India's library movement led by S. R. Ranganathan ("father of library science", Colon Classification, Five Laws of Library Science, 1931); the Madras Public Libraries Act (1948).
  • Paperback revolution: Penguin Books (1935, Allen Lane); Indian publishers such as Rajkamal Prakashan (1947), Hind Pocket Books (1958, pioneered Hindi paperbacks), National Book Trust (1957).
  • Literacy: India's literacy rose from about 18% (1951 census) to 74% (2011 census).

  • Project Gutenberg (1971), the first e-library; the ISBN (international from 1970).
  • Online bookselling: Amazon (1995); Flipkart started as an online bookshop (2007).
  • E-readers: Sony Reader (2006), Amazon Kindle (2007); Google Books scanning (2004).
  • Audiobooks and podcasts: Audible (1995), Storytel; Indian-language audio platforms.
  • Web fiction and self-publishing: Kindle Direct Publishing (2007), Wattpad (2006), Pratilipi (2014), Chinese web literature.
  • Digital libraries: National Digital Library of India (IIT Kharagpur), Internet Archive, HathiTrust, Europeana, the Digital Library of India.
  • AI era (2020s): AI writing, translation and narration tools; lawsuits and debates on training data and authorship (BOK-19.5).

sections.title: Literary ages and movements
sections.html:
Before you start — BOK-13. Movements are groups of writers who share a style, a purpose or a rebellion. Indian literature has its own movements, which often ran in parallel with or answered European ones. See also: MOV-08 Film movements, MUS (song movements).

  • Sangam age (Tamil, about 300 BCE to 300 CE).
  • Classical Sanskrit kavya (about 1st to 12th century).
  • Bhakti movement (Tamil Nadu from the 6th century, then across India to the 17th): devotion in the people's languages; Alvars, Nayanars, Basavanna, Dnyaneshwar, Kabir, Ravidas, Surdas, Tulsidas, Meera, Chaitanya, Sankardev, Guru Nanak.
  • Sufi poetry: Amir Khusrau, Bulleh Shah, Shah Latif, Lal Ded's mystic kin.
  • Riti kal (Hindi court poetry, about 1650–1850).
  • Bengal Renaissance (19th century): Rammohun Roy, Vidyasagar, Bankim, Tagore.
  • Nationalist literature: "Vande Mataram", Bharati, Maithili Sharan Gupt (Bharat-Bharati), Makhanlal Chaturvedi, Subhadra Kumari Chauhan ("Jhansi ki Rani").
  • Chhayavad (Hindi romanticism, 1918–1936): Prasad, Nirala, Pant, Mahadevi Verma.
  • Progressive Writers' Movement (1936): literature for social change; Premchand, Faiz, Mulk Raj Anand, Sajjad Zaheer.
  • Prayogvad and Nayi Kavita (from 1943): Agyeya's Tar Saptak, experimental Hindi poetry.
  • Nayi Kahani (1950s): Mohan Rakesh, Kamleshwar, Rajendra Yadav.
  • Hungry Generation (Bengali, 1961) and Digambara poets (Telugu, 1965): angry avant-garde poetry.
  • Navya (Kannada modernism): Gopalakrishna Adiga, U. R. Ananthamurthy.
  • Dalit literature (Marathi from the 1960s, then all languages): Ambedkarite writing of dignity and protest.
  • Feminist and women's writing: Ismat Chughtai, Kamala Das, Mahasweta Devi, Ambai, Mridula Garg; Kali for Women (1984), India's first feminist press.
  • Indian English "Midnight's children" generation (from 1981).
  • Adivasi and North-east literatures (21st century).

  • Classical (Greece and Rome): order, balance, imitation of nature.
  • Medieval (about 500–1400): romance, allegory, courtly love, the troubadours.
  • Renaissance (about 1300–1650): humanism; Petrarch, Shakespeare, Cervantes.
  • Baroque and Neoclassicism (17th–18th century): Molière, Pope, Racine.
  • Enlightenment (18th century): reason and satire; Voltaire, Swift.
  • Romanticism (about 1790–1850): feeling, nature, the individual; Wordsworth, Goethe, Pushkin. Inspired by translated Sanskrit literature (Shakuntala and the Gita).
  • Realism and Naturalism (about 1830–1900): Balzac, Flaubert, Tolstoy, Zola.
  • Symbolism and Aestheticism (late 19th century): Baudelaire, Mallarmé, Oscar Wilde.
  • Modernism (about 1900–1945): breaking forms; Joyce, Woolf, Eliot, Kafka, Proust.
  • Harlem Renaissance (1920s): Black American voices.
  • Négritude (1930s): Césaire, Senghor.
  • Existentialism and the Absurd (1940s–50s): Sartre, Camus, Beckett.
  • The Beat Generation (1950s): Ginsberg, Kerouac; some travelled in India.
  • Latin American Boom and magical realism (1960s–70s).
  • Postmodernism (from the 1960s): irony, play, metafiction; Pynchon, Calvino, Rushdie.
  • Postcolonial literature (from the 1950s): Achebe, Ngũgĩ, Walcott, Rushdie, Roy.
  • Contemporary trends (21st century): autofiction (Knausgård, Annie Ernaux), climate fiction, translated fiction boom, BookTok-driven bestsellers.

sections.title: Authors: the people of literature
sections.html:
Before you start — BOK-14. A selection of writers whose work shaped literature, sorted by role. Each name gets a profile page on the website with life, major works, a short reading path and sources. Many more appear in the language sections of Part 1. See also: BOK-15 Nobel laureates, BOK-16.1 Jnanpith winners.

  • Enheduanna (Sumer): first named author. Homer (Greece): the epics. Valmiki and Vyasa (India, by tradition): the epics. Confucius and Laozi (China). Sappho (Greece): lyric. Kalidasa (India): poet-dramatist. Thiruvalluvar (Tamil): the Kural.

  • Andal, Basavanna, Akka Mahadevi, Lal Ded, Kabir, Ravidas, Meera, Surdas, Tulsidas, Tukaram, Guru Nanak, Rumi, Hafez, Amir Khusrau, Bulleh Shah: poets who spoke directly to God in the people's language.

  • Murasaki Shikibu, Cervantes, Cao Xueqin, Austen, Dickens, Tolstoy, Dostoevsky, George Eliot, Flaubert, Hugo, Twain, Proust, Joyce, Woolf, Kafka, Thomas Mann, Faulkner, García Márquez, Achebe, Mahfouz, Morrison, Kawabata, Murakami.

  • Bankim Chandra, Tagore, Sarat Chandra, Premchand, Fakir Mohan Senapati, Bibhutibhushan, R. K. Narayan, Manto, Ismat Chughtai, Qurratulain Hyder, Thakazhi, Basheer, Shivaram Karanth, U. R. Ananthamurthy, Mahasweta Devi, Krishna Sobti, Nirmal Verma, Vijaydan Detha, O. V. Vijayan, Salman Rushdie, Amitav Ghosh, Arundhati Roy, Perumal Murugan, Geetanjali Shree, Banu Mushtaq.

  • Enheduanna, Sappho, Murasaki Shikibu, Akka Mahadevi, Meera, Mary Wollstonecraft, Jane Austen, Mary Shelley, the Brontës, George Eliot, Emily Dickinson, Virginia Woolf, Mahadevi Verma, Amrita Pritam, Ismat Chughtai, Toni Morrison, Kamala Das, Mahasweta Devi, Maya Angelou, Margaret Atwood, Wisława Szymborska, Han Kang, Annie Ernaux; and Tarabai Shinde, whose Stri Purush Tulana (1882) is an early Indian feminist text.

  • Kumarajiva and Xuanzang (Sanskrit to Chinese), Ibn al-Muqaffa (Panchatantra into Arabic), Dara Shikoh (Upanishads into Persian, 1657), William Jones and Charles Wilkins (Sanskrit into English), Edward FitzGerald, Constance Garnett (Russian), A. parts.title: Awards, Prizes and Records
parts.intro: About this Part. Each award has the same card: who gives it, since when, for what, the first winner, landmark winners and the latest winner, with the date it was checked. Prizes are a guide, not a verdict: many great writers (Tolstoy, Joyce, Premchand) never won the big international prizes. Latest winners were checked on the web on 3 November 2026. Where a result was due after that date, the card says so.

sections.title: International literary prizes
sections.html:
Before you start — BOK-15. Some prizes honour a writer's whole body of work (the Nobel), others a single book (the Booker). Some are open only to English (the Booker), others to translations (the International Booker). See also: MOV-10 Film awards (for the same card format).

Given by the Swedish Academy since 1901 under Alfred Nobel's will, to an author for the body of work "in an ideal direction". First winner: Sully Prudhomme (France, 1901). Landmarks: Rabindranath Tagore (1913, first non-European), Selma Lagerlöf (1909, first woman), Wole Soyinka (1986, first African), Toni Morrison (1993), Bob Dylan (2016, songwriter), Han Kang (2024, first Asian woman). Latest: Anne Carson (Canada, poet, essayist and classicist), announced 8 October 2026; before her, László Krasznahorkai (Hungary, 2025). Tags: #nobel #award

  • Indian-born or Indian-origin laureates: Rabindranath Tagore (1913); Rudyard Kipling (1907, born in Bombay); V. S. Naipaul (2001, Indo-Trinidadian).
  • Prizes not awarded: in some war years and in 2018 (a Swedish Academy scandal; two prizes given in 2019).
  • Declined: Boris Pasternak (1958, forced by Soviet authorities) and Jean-Paul Sartre (1964, by choice).

sections.title: National literary awards, country by country
sections.html:
Before you start — BOK-16. National awards honour a country's own literature. India's are unusual because they cover many languages at once. See also: Exam Guide (awards are a favourite topic in competitive exams).

  • Jnanpith Award (Bharatiya Jnanpith, first given 1965): India's highest literary award, for a writer's outstanding contribution in any Eighth Schedule language or in English. First winner: G. Sankara Kurup (Malayalam, Odakkuzhal, 1965). Landmarks: Ashapurna Devi (1976, first woman), Amitav Ghosh (2018, first English writer), Gulzar (Urdu) and Jagadguru Rambhadracharya (Sanskrit) shared the 58th (2023). Latest: 59th (2024) Vinod Kumar Shukla (Hindi); 60th (2025) R. Vairamuthu (Tamil poet and film lyricist), announced 14 March 2026.
  • Sahitya Akademi Award (National Academy of Letters, established 1954; awards since 1955): one book a year in each of 24 languages. First Hindi winner: Makhanlal Chaturvedi (1955, Him Taringini). Latest (2025 awards, announced 16 March 2026): English: Navtej Sarna, Crimson Spring (novel); Hindi: Mamta Kalia, Jeete Jee Allahabad (memoir); Rajasthani: Jitender Kumar Soni, Bharkham; Tamil: Sa. Tamilselvan; Bengali: Prasun Bandyopadhyay; Urdu: Pritpal Singh Betab.
  • Sahitya Akademi Fellowship: the Akademi's highest honour, for "immortals of literature"; first fellow S. Radhakrishnan (1968).
  • Sahitya Akademi Yuva Puraskar (2011): writers under 35. Bal Sahitya Puraskar (2010): children's literature. Translation Prize (1989).
  • Saraswati Samman (K. K. Birla Foundation, 1991): for a work in any Eighth Schedule language. First winner: Harivansh Rai Bachchan (Hindi, autobiography). Latest: 2025 to Ramkumar Mukhopadhyay for the Bengali novel Hara Parbati Katha (announced March 2026); 2024 to Mahamahopadhyay Bhadreshdas Swami (Sanskrit), the first saint-scholar to receive it.
  • Vyas Samman (K. K. Birla Foundation, 1991): Hindi literature; first winner Ram Vilas Sharma.
  • Bihari Puraskar (K. K. Birla Foundation, 1991): Hindi and Rajasthani writers of Rajasthan.
  • JCB Prize for Literature (2018–): fiction by an Indian writer, including translations; first winner Benyamin's Jasmine Days (tr. Shahnaz Habib). Later winners include Perumal Murugan's Fire Bird (2023, tr. Janani Kannan). Latest edition: to be checked.

sections.title: Best-sellers, records and numbers
sections.html:
Before you start — BOK-17. Sales figures for books are estimates, often from publishers' own claims, and are hard to compare across centuries and languages. Treat every number as approximate and check its source. See also: MOV-13 Film records.

  • The Bible: estimated billions of copies; full translations in more than 700 languages (Wycliffe Global Alliance).
  • The Qur'an, the Bhagavad Gita, the Ramcharitmanas, the Hanuman Chalisa (Gita Press, Gorakhpur, founded 1923, has printed hundreds of millions of copies of Hindu texts).
  • Quotations from Chairman Mao (the "Little Red Book"): estimates of about a billion copies.
  • Most translated single literary work besides scripture: Antoine de Saint-Exupéry's The Little Prince (1943), in over 500 languages and dialects; Carlo Collodi's Pinocchio is close behind.
  • Most translated author (UNESCO Index Translationum, data up to the 2010s): Agatha Christie, then Jules Verne and Shakespeare.

  • Don Quixote (claimed 500 million), A Tale of Two Cities (about 200 million), The Little Prince (about 200 million), Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone (over 120 million), The Hobbit, And Then There Were None (about 100 million), The Alchemist (over 150 million claimed by the author's publishers).
  • Best-selling series: Harry Potter (over 600 million copies across seven books, according to its publishers).
  • India: Chandrakanta, Godaan, the Gita Press editions, Chetan Bhagat's novels, Amish's Shiva Trilogy, Wings of Fire, NCERT textbooks and exam guides (the true best-sellers by volume).

  • Longest epic: the Kyrgyz Manas and the Tibetan Epic of King Gesar are often called longer than the Mahabharata (about 100,000 shlokas in the full tradition, or about 1.8 million words), depending on how versions are counted.
  • Largest library: the Library of Congress (more than 170 million items); India's largest is the National Library, Kolkata.
  • Largest book fairs: Frankfurt Book Fair (the biggest trade fair), Kolkata International Book Fair (among the largest by visitors), New Delhi World Book Fair (since 1972, organised by the National Book Trust).
  • Oldest continuously operating library: the al-Qarawiyyin library in Fez, Morocco (founded 859).
  • India's publishing size: India is one of the largest book markets and English-language publishers in the world; figures vary by report (Federation of Indian Publishers, Nielsen), so the website will cite the latest dated report.

parts.title: The Craft and the Business of Books
parts.intro: About this Part. How a book comes into being: written, edited, designed, printed, translated, sold, kept in libraries and protected by law. This is the "behind the scenes" of literature.

sections.title: The craft of writing
sections.html:
Before you start — BOK-18. Every book is built from a few basic tools: story, character, point of view, voice, structure and style. Knowing them makes you a sharper reader and a better writer. See also: MOV-15 (screenwriting), BOK-20 Theory.

  • Plot: the order of events; Aristotle's beginning, middle and end; Freytag's pyramid (exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, resolution).
  • Character: round and flat (E. M. Forster, Aspects of the Novel, 1927), protagonist and antagonist, the character arc.
  • Setting: time and place; Malgudi, Macondo and Middle-earth as places readers "visit".
  • Point of view: first person ("I"), third person limited or omniscient, second person ("you"), unreliable narrator.
  • Theme: the big idea underneath; love, power, death, freedom, identity.
  • Conflict: person against person, nature, society, self or fate.
  • Structure patterns: the hero's journey (Joseph Campbell, The Hero with a Thousand Faces, 1949), three-act structure, frame tales, non-linear stories.

  • Figures of speech (alankara): simile (upama), metaphor (rupaka), personification, hyperbole (atishayokti), alliteration (anuprasa), pun (shlesha), irony.
  • Imagery and symbol; tone and mood; diction (word choice); rhythm in prose.
  • Dialogue: how people talk on the page; dialect writing (Renu, Twain).
  • Show, don't tell: let readers infer feelings from action and detail.

  • Drafting and revising: most books go through many drafts; famous writers' routines (Premchand wrote daily; Hemingway stopped mid-sentence to restart next day).
  • Writing workshops and programmes: Iowa Writers' Workshop (1936), creative writing courses in India (Ashoka, Jadavpur), Sahitya Akademi workshops.
  • Writer's block, reading as training, keeping a notebook.
  • Writing in your mother tongue: why many writers, from Ngũgĩ to Premchand (who moved from Urdu to Hindi), thought deeply about language choice.
